newsitem.title: BULGARIA: CHANCES OF BULGARIA'S DEBT DEFAULT RISE.
newsitem.headline: CHANCES OF BULGARIA'S DEBT DEFAULT RISE.

text.p: Chances have increased of Bulgaria becoming the first country to default on a Brady debt restructuring deal as economic recovery remains remote and is strongly linked to external funding, investors say.

"It is unclear yet whether there is internal or external support for Bulgaria defaulting, but it would set a precedent as this would be the first Brady deal to default," said David Boren, vice president of Salomon Brothers emerging markets research.

He was speaking at a closed-door seminar in Sofia over the weekend, organised by the Institute for Market Economy, a local think-tank, which discussed Bulgaria's ability to sustain future debt payments.
"There is not a conscious political force driving the country to default, but with its current economic deadlock it is headed towards default," said IME director Krassen Stanchev.

Brady bonds provided emerging economies in Eastern Europe and Latin America with a mechanism for restructuring foreign debt burdens. Named for former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, they are also traded on the secondary debt market.

Bulgaria issued some $5 billion worth of Brady bonds in 1994 as part of an $8.16 billion foreign commercial debt restructuring deal but its economy failed to meet projections mapped out under that London Club accord.
Optimistic scenarios assumed growth of around two percent in 1996 and up to 3.2 percent in 1997.

Bulgaria now expects zero growth this year and economists see negative growth for next year, as contined delay to implement structural reforms, foster economic growth and attract foreign investment has undercut the effect of initially successful monetary reforms.

One quarter of Bulgaria's banks are in receivership and last month's introduction of a drastic 300 percent main interest rate has so far failed to restore much confidence in the crumbling financial system.
Under pressure to ease investment in the stagnant real economy, the central bank cut the rate to 240 percent last week.
An International Monetary Fund mission due in Sofia this week or early next week will evaluate the government's success in closing down loss-making state enterprises and speeding up privatisation.
The Fund is then expected to decide on a crucial $115 million funding tranche, twice postponed so far due to Sofia's slow reform performance.
Bulgarian officials have said it is important to receive the IMF funding by year-end as the next Brady coupon payments of around $130 million are due at the end of January.
Bulgaria's medium-term ability to service its external debt fully depends on a sustainable export-driven economic recovery and rising foreign investment, analysts said.
Exports declined by 17 percent for the first half of the year due to a slumping lev, because Bulgarian exports contain imported components, one IME expert told the seminar.
Bulgaria suffers the lowest level of foreign investment in the region, behind countries like Hungary and Romania.
Foreign exchange reserves have fallen to $506 million in September, a slump from even the most pessimistic scenarios for 1996 which had placed them at around $900 million.
"As winter months imports increase significantly they will erode the reserves further," said a central bank official attending the seminar.
The country needs around $350 million by year-end to cover current expenses, which include fuel and grain supplies. Foreign debt payments due until end-1996 amount to around a further $150 million.
Dues to government and bank creditors in the first quarter of 1997 total $300 million or some 30 percent of all debt payments for next year, said the central bank official.
"It would be better if the goverment announced default as early as possible, so that negotiations on a new restructuring deal would begin immediately," said an investor.
Restructuring of Bulgaria's Brady deal could last longer than a year, said another investor.
Foreign debt to gross domestic product ratio stood at 76.4 percent in 1995.
"If you look at the Brady market, the Bulgarian Bradies are priced in anticipation of default," said one investor, who declined to be named.
